arrive: Day three. Resting on power. Today goes deep instead of wide: one home station, dwelt in. First the soak — four voices on power, then your own. Then the sit. Speech windows are optional everywhere: if words are there, tap, and speak them. Nothing to achieve. Begin when you're ready.
soak_intro: The soak. Your pen from yesterday — I just don't see a problem with aggressive power in the right context — is today's question. Four voices circle it: how do you tell real power from its counterfeit, from inside?
soak1: First voice. Blackstone — the real thing. Our actual quality of power requires no effort; it is just naturally there within our body. It is generally a settled, gentle feeling of personal strength, rather than an active state. As an internal quality, rather than an outward attitude, we can rest on, or in, our own power. This allows us to feel equal to other people, without effort, and to feel supported by our own inner strength.
soak1_verify: Her core line, once more: real power requires no effort. We can rest on it, or in it.
soak2: Second voice. Blackstone — the counterfeit. Some people defend against this vulnerability by attempting to produce a facsimile of power in other parts of their body — for example, by pushing forward with their forehead, or their upper chest. Although this compensatory organization may be intimidating to others, it is a defensive artifice, and does not truly feel like strength. It is also exhausting to maintain, even if we are not aware that we are holding ourselves in this way.
soak2_verify: The counterfeit, from inside: it pushes, it doesn't rest — and it exhausts.
soak3: Third voice. Chapman, from the essay called Power. Power is the ability to get things done. Power makes it possible to benefit others, and to change the world for the better. On the other hand, power corrupts. Power is, at best, morally neutral. Power is not nice. Power is not polite. Power can't be wished out of existence. We're stuck with it. Better to see it clearly, and to use it effectively. Power from within grants the ability to make elegant, accurate, kind, effective, expansive changes in the world. The more power you have, the more emotionally mature you have to be to use it properly. Nobility is right use of power.
soak3_verify: Where the essay lands: nobility is right use of power.
soak4: Fourth voice. Chapman again — wrathful practice. The tradition that says yes to ferocity, and the price tag on the label. If you are sufficiently committed, you can deliberately stir up negative emotions in order to transform them. With this practice, hatred can be transformed into the clarity of enlightenment. Destruction is one of the four functions of a Buddha. Wrathful practice gives you the clarity to know what must be destroyed, and the ferocity to destroy it. The serious risk, is that you will fail in the transformation — and fail to see that you have failed.
soak4_verify: Ferocity is usable — and its signature failure is invisible from inside. That is what makes Blackstone's distinction an instrument, rather than a preference.
soak5: The fifth voice is yours. From yesterday's say-it-back: If you are grounded within your natural power, you're far less likely to have these unknown wants leaking. Resting within that feeling of personal strength, it would have been easier to see both of those clearly, and not have the perceptual flinch. So — after the four voices: where does aggressive power, in the right context, land now?
practice_intro: The sit. Midsection-anchored — one home station, dwelt in. Each dwell runs the length you set; the chime is permission, not a demand. An open dwell ends when you tap. Stopping at today's edge is the practice succeeding.
st_settle: Settle. Sit with your back straight and your feet on the floor. Close your eyes. Begin by feeling that you are inside your feet, that you inhabit them. Let your breath adjust to you being in your feet, so that your inhale does not lift you up away from them. Now feel that you inhabit your whole body at once. Sit for a moment, living within your whole body.
st_power: Midsection — power at home. Inhabit your midsection, between your ribs and your pelvis. Attune to the quality of power within your midsection — pure, natural power, like the power of a waterfall. It requires no effort; it is just naturally there: a settled, gentle feeling of personal strength, rather than an active state. Let yourself rest on, or in, your own power. Bring your breath down into your midsection, and feel it move through the quality of power.
st_dimmer: The dimmer. She says we have a kind of dimmer button on all of these qualities. Still in your midsection: gently intensify the quality of power — the way she did across from Louise: don't let me overpower you. Then let it settle back to its natural level. Both settings are the same power. While it is turned up, run the counterfeit check: is the forehead, or the upper chest, pushing forward to help? Let them stand down — the midsection doesn't need them. The difference between intensifying and pushing is today's whole soak, felt.
st_blend: Desire joins. Now attune to the raw quality of desire within your midsection — wanting itself, before any object. Let the two join: the quality of desire settling on, and supported by, the quality of power. No separation between qualities, no need to choose. Wanting, with a spine under it. Bring your breath down into your midsection, and feel it move through both at once.
st_border: No clear border. Your own pen from yesterday: there might even be no clear border. Test it. Widen to your pelvis, midsection, and chest at once — desire at its foundation, power at its home, the little tenderness in the chest. Look for the seam where one quality ends and another begins. A border, a gradient, or nothing at all — whatever you find, is the finding.
st_ask: An ask arrives. Resting on power, desire joined: let a mild ask from another person come to mind — someone wants something from you, or is quietly disappointed. The salesperson moment, re-run on your own terms. Don't manage it. Just watch whether both wants stay visible — the want for their happiness, and the want to decline. If the flinch comes, don't fight it; notice where it lands — the throat? the head? — and whether the midsection stays findable underneath it. Then let the person go, and re-settle.
st_own: Optional — your own situation. This one is yours to skip if today isn't the day. Bring a second situation of your own — one where staying in your power would have helped you stay within your desire, without being dependent on the outcome. Same shape: rest on power, let the situation arrive, and feel the want as a want — free-standing, yours, whether or not it gets its object. If wanting-without-getting collapses into managing, or solving, that's the counterfeit sneaking back. Return to the midsection, and rest.
st_everything: Everything. Find the space outside your body, the space in the room. Feel that the space inside and outside of your body is the same continuous space. Slowly open your eyes. Without moving at all from within your body, attune to the space — and the quality of desire — pervading your body and everything in your environment, at the same time. Experience everything as desire. And if it is available: let the whole field rest the way your midsection rests — everything as desire, resting on power.
prompt_generic: If words are there — tap, and speak. Or continue.
prompt_dimmer: Intensifying, versus pushing — what was the difference? Tap, and speak. Or continue.
prompt_border: What did the border turn out to be? Tap, and speak.
prompt_ask: Did both wants stay visible? What did the flinch do? Tap, and speak.
sayitback: Say it back. Blackstone splits real power from its counterfeit by feel: one rests; one pushes, and exhausts. Chapman keeps ferocity on the menu, and names its signature risk: failing at the transformation, and not seeing that you've failed. In your own words: how do you tell, from inside, whether force is coming from the ground, or from the push? Take your time. Tap, and speak, when ready.
sayitback_sources: The sources, for your version to stand against. Blackstone: our actual quality of power requires no effort. We can rest on, or in, our own power. And: a defensive artifice, that does not truly feel like strength — exhausting to maintain. Chapman: the serious risk is that you will fail in the transformation, and fail to see that you have failed. And: nobility, is right use of power.
prompt_feedback: Last window — feedback for the build. What worked, what didn't, what should tomorrow be? Tap, and speak.
close: That's the day. The field note stays in the field: when a real ask arrives, check the midsection first — is power findable there, in the moment? Does finding it change what happens in the throat, and the head? Export your transcript when you're ready. See you at day four.
